qs.q: A 62-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B develops hepatocellular carcinoma with inactivation of the p53 gene. Which of the following is the normal cellular function of p53?
o: Induction of local angiogenesis through VEGF secretion
Induction of apoptosis in cells with irreparable DNA damage
Direct repair of DNA double-strand breaks
Phosphorylation of RB to permit cell cycle progression
qs.e: p53 normally halts the cell cycle for DNA repair; if damage is unfixable, it triggers apoptosis. Losing p53 allows genetically damaged cells to survive and accumulate further mutations.
qs.s: Pathology by Dr. Irungu — — Oncopathology: MCQs

qs.q: A pregnant woman who is a chronic hepatitis B carrier gives birth and asks whether she can safely breastfeed her newborn. Assuming the infant receives appropriate immunoprophylaxis at delivery, what is the best recommendation regarding feeding?
qs.e: Breastfeeding does not increase the risk of vertical transmission of hepatitis B when the infant receives post-exposure immunoprophylaxis at birth. Formula feeding is not required solely due to maternal carrier status.
qs.s: Master Rhinoviruses & RVFV: Common Cold & Zoonotic Fever: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with chronic hepatitis B undergoes evaluation to understand the mechanism of hepatocellular injury. What is the primary driver of hepatocellular damage in hepatitis B infections?
o: Secondary bacterial superinfection of bile ducts.
Direct toxic breakdown of hepatocyte membranes by viral DNA.
Direct cytopathic effect of viral replication.
Host immune response to infected hepatocytes.
qs.e: Hepatocellular damage in hepatitis B is caused primarily by the host immune response attacking infected liver cells rather than a direct viral cytopathic effect. This immune-mediated clearance contributes to both recovery and chronic inflammation.
qs.s: Master Rhinoviruses & RVFV: Common Cold & Zoonotic Fever: MCQs

qs.q: An unvaccinated adult presents with profound fatigue, dark urine, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Serology confirms acute hepatitis B. Approximately what percentage of infected adult patients progress to chronic hepatitis B?
o: Five percent progress to chronic infection.
Ninety percent progress to chronic infection.
Seventy percent progress to chronic infection.
Zero percent progress to chronic infection.
qs.e: Approximately 5% of infected adults progress to chronic hepatitis B, whereas about 90% of infected infants develop chronic infection. Adults typically clear the acute infection more efficiently than neonates.
qs.s: Master Rhinoviruses & RVFV: Common Cold & Zoonotic Fever: MCQs

qs.q: An infant born to an HBV-infected mother acquires the virus during delivery. What is the approximate probability that this infant will develop a chronic hepatitis B infection?
qs.e: Approximately 90% of infants infected with hepatitis B progress to chronic infection, compared to only about 5% of infected adults. This high chronicity rate highlights the importance of vertical transmission prevention.
qs.s: Master Rhinoviruses & RVFV: Common Cold & Zoonotic Fever: MCQs

qs.q: Which drug class is utilized for the lifelong management of chronic hepatitis B by inhibiting viral replication through DNA polymerase suppression?
qs.e: DNA polymerase inhibitors such as tenofovir, lamivudine, adefovir, and entecavir are given lifelong for chronic hepatitis B management. Interferons are typically given for a fixed duration of six months.
qs.s: Master Rhinoviruses & RVFV: Common Cold & Zoonotic Fever: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with chronic hepatitis B is co-infected with Hepatitis C. What is the primary clinical consequence of this specific viral dual infection on the liver?
o: Lower risk of progression to cirrhosis
qs.e: Co-infection with HBV and HCV leads to an increased rate of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and worsened liver disease outcomes. Similar synergistic malignancy risks occur with HBV and HDV.
qs.s: Master Rhinoviruses & RVFV: Common Cold & Zoonotic Fever: MCQs

qs.q: When reviewing extra-hepatic manifestations of chronic hepatitis B infection, which of the following organ systems is classically affected by immune-complex deposition leading to glomerulonephritis?
qs.e: Renal involvement in chronic hepatitis B manifests as glomerulonephritis due to extra-hepatic immune complex deposition. Other extra-hepatic signs include arthralgia, myocarditis, and pleural effusions.
qs.s: Master Rhinoviruses & RVFV: Common Cold & Zoonotic Fever: MCQs

es.q: A 65-year-old male with a long history of chronic Hepatitis C infection presents with progressive fatigue, confusion, abdominal distension, and easy bruising. Discuss the definition and major causes of hepatic failure, and elaborate on the key clinical consequences associated with this condition, ex
es.m: Hepatic failure is defined as the loss of 80-90% of hepatic functional capacity. es.q: A liver biopsy from a patient with chronic hepatitis shows areas of periportal necrosis and significant collagen deposition. Identify the specific histologic patterns described and explain their significance in chronic liver disease progression.
es.m: The periportal necrosis is referred to as 'piecemeal necrosis,' which is characteristic of chronic hepatitis. The 'collagen deposition' signifies fibrosis. Both findings are indicative of ongoing liver injury and the initiation of a scarring process that, if uncontrolled, can progress to cirrhosis.

ai.title: Chronic Hepatitis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Chronic hepatitis is persistent liver inflammation, most often due to hepatitis B or C, that can progress to fibrosis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Diagnosis relies on serology, viral load and liver assessment, while management focuses on antiviral therapy, monitoring and prevention of complications.

sections.p: Chronic hepatitis is defined as liver inflammation lasting >6 months, usually confirmed by persistent HBsAg or anti‑HCV antibodies together with elevated ALT/AST or histologic activity.
b: HBsAg positive >6 months → chronic hepatitis B
Anti‑HCV positive + RNA detectable → chronic hepatitis C

t.b: Is the infection chronic? Positive HBsAg or anti‑HCV with RNA confirms chronic disease
Is there active hepatocellular injury? ALT >2× ULN suggests active inflammation

t.a: HBV DNA or HCV RNA quantification
t.b: What is viral replication level? High HBV DNA (>20,000 IU/mL) or HCV RNA (>800,000 IU/mL) guides treatment urgency
What is fibrosis stage? FibroScan ≥9.5 kPa or APRI ≥1.0 indicates significant fibrosis
Is there hepatocellular carcinoma? Any focal lesion or AFP >400 ng/mL warrants further imaging

sections.p: Severity is staged by fibrosis (METAVIR F0‑F4) and activity (A0‑A3). Cirrhosis (F4) carries risk of decompensation and HCC.
b: F0‑F1: minimal fibrosis – monitor
F2‑F3: moderate‑advanced fibrosis – consider antiviral therapy
F4: cirrhosis – start antiviral, screen for HCC, vaccinate against HAV/HBV

sections.p: In East Africa the dominant causes are viral, but co‑factors are common.
b: Hepatitis B (endemic, perinatal or early childhood exposure)
Hepatitis C (injecting drug use, unsafe medical injections)
HIV co‑infection (accelerates fibrosis)
Schistosoma mansoni (hepatic periportal fibrosis)
Traditional herbal remedies (hepatotoxic alkaloids)
Alcoholic liver disease (often co‑exists)
Non‑alcoholic fatty liver disease (rising with urbanisation)

sections.p: Most patients are asymptomatic; when symptoms appear they are vague and reflect progressive liver injury.
b: Fatigue, anorexia, mild right‑upper‑quadrant discomfort
Occasional jaundice when bilirubin rises
Signs of chronic liver disease: spider naevi, palmar erythema, hepatomegaly

sections.p: Select tests that answer the key clinical questions; when a test is unavailable, use clinical surrogates.

t.b: Is infection chronic? Positive result confirms chronic hepatitis B or C

t.a: HBV DNA or HCV RNA PCR
t.b: What is viral load? Guides need for antiviral therapy; if PCR unavailable, use ALT trend as proxy
Is there active inflammation? ALT >2× ULN indicates active disease
Is there synthetic dysfunction? Low platelets, INR >1.5, albumin <35 g/L suggest cirrhosis
What is fibrosis stage when FibroScan unavailable? APRI ≥1.0 or FIB‑4 ≥3.25 indicates significant fibrosis
Is HCC present? Any focal lesion or AFP >400 ng/mL prompts CT/MRI

sections.p: Identify patients at risk of rapid decompensation or death.
b: Ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, variceal bleeding – decompensated cirrhosis
Sudden rise in bilirubin >5 mg/dL
AFP >400 ng/mL or new liver mass – possible HCC
Coagulopathy (INR >1.5) with bleeding

sections.p: Treat the underlying virus, support liver function and prevent complications.
b: Tenofovir or entecavir for chronic hepatitis B – potent, low resistance, safe in renal impairment
Pegylated interferon‑α or direct‑acting antivirals (sofosbuvir/ledipasvir) for hepatitis C – cure rates >95 %
Avoid hepatotoxic drugs (e.g., isoniazid without pyridoxine, high‑dose paracetamol)
Vaccinate against HAV and HBV (if not immune)
Manage portal hypertension: non‑selective beta‑blockers, endoscopic variceal ligation
Screen for HCC with ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months in cirrhosis

sections.p: Long‑term monitoring prevents progression and detects complications early.
b: HBV DNA every 6–12 months; HCV RNA at end of therapy and 12 weeks after
ALT/AST and liver panel every 3–6 months
FibroScan or APRI annually to track fibrosis
Ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months if F4
Counselling on safe injection practices, condom use, and avoidance of unregulated herbal medicines
Alcoholic hepatitis – history of heavy alcohol use, AST:ALT ratio >2
Non‑alcoholic fatty liver disease – metabolic risk factors, ultrasound steatosis without viral markers
Autoimmune hepatitis – positive ANA/ASMA, hypergammaglobulinemia
Normal ALT does not exclude significant fibrosis; rely on elastography or APRI
Low HBV DNA in immune‑tolerant phase may still progress; consider age and fibrosis
AFP can be normal in early HCC; imaging is essential

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly rising AFP or new liver mass

faq.q: Why is tenofovir preferred over lamivudine for chronic hepatitis B?
faq.a: Tenofovir has a higher barrier to resistance and better viral suppression, especially important in low‑resource settings where monitoring is limited.

faq.q: Can a patient with normal ALT still have cirrhosis?
faq.a: Yes; fibrosis can progress silently. Imaging or elastography is needed to assess stage.

faq.q: When is liver biopsy still required?
faq.a: When non‑invasive scores are inconclusive and the result will change management, such as distinguishing autoimmune hepatitis from viral disease.

exam: A 32‑year‑old man with HBsAg positive for 8 years presents with fatigue. ALT is 45 U/L (ULN 40). What is the next step — assess fibrosis with FibroScan or APRI before deciding on antiviral therapy.
A patient with chronic hepatitis C is pregnant. Which antiviral is contraindicated and why — ribavirin is avoided because of teratogenicity; defer treatment until postpartum.
You see a cirrhotic patient with new upper‑GI bleed. What immediate management is required — resuscitate, give IV octreotide, start prophylactic antibiotics, arrange urgent endoscopy.
A 45‑year‑old with chronic hepatitis B has HBV DNA 100 million IU/mL but normal ALT. How do you justify treatment — high viral load in a patient >30 years old predicts progression; start tenofovir.
How does schistosomiasis contribute to chronic hepatitis in East Africa — periportal fibrosis from S. mansoni adds to portal hypertension and can mimic viral cirrhosis.
Explain why AFP alone is insufficient for HCC screening in cirrhosis — AFP can be normal in early HCC; ultrasound provides structural detection.
A patient on tenofovir develops rising creatinine. What alternative antiviral can be used and why — switch to entecavir, which has less renal toxicity, provided no resistance.
What lifestyle advice reduces progression of chronic hepatitis — avoid alcohol, maintain healthy weight, vaccinate against HAV/HBV, limit hepatotoxic herbs.
